title: Supreme Court Overturns 91-Year Precedent, Grants Trump Sweeping Power to Fire Independent Agency Leaders
summary:
The Supreme Court delivered a transformative victory to the Trump administration on Thursday, ruling that the president can fire members of independent agencies without cause. The 6-3 decision explicitly overruled Humphrey's Executor, the 1935 precedent that had protected commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission and similar bodies from at-will removal for 91 years.

The case centered on Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, a Democratic FTC commissioner appointed in 2018. President Trump fired her in March 2025, stating only that her "continued service on the FTC is inconsistent with [the] Administration's priorities." Congress had designed the FTC to be bipartisan and insulated from political pressure: commissioners serve staggered terms and can be removed only for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office." A lower court found Slaughter's firing unlawful under Humphrey's Executor.

Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the conservative majority, rejected that reasoning. "Subordinates who exercise the President's power are subject to removal by him," Roberts wrote. "Then, and only then, can they remain accountable to the President, and the President to the people." He emphasized that the modern FTC wields substantial executive authority, enforcing some 80 statutes across the economy — making it, in the Court's view, fundamentally an executive agency.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor's dissent was scathing. She called the decision "grievously wrong" and said it gives the president "a power unknown even to the English Crown against which the Founders revolted." She argued the ruling elevates the president above the other branches by allowing him to defy laws Congress passed to ensure agency independence.

The practical impact is immediate and far-reaching. FTC commissioners now serve at the president's pleasure. The statutory requirement that no more than three of the five commissioners belong to the same party is effectively void, since a president could simply fire commissioners from the opposing party and nominate loyalists. The FTC's antitrust and consumer protection work — policing tech giants, pharmaceutical companies, and media conglomerates — could shift dramatically with each administration.

This ruling follows a pattern: during Trump's first term, the Court allowed him to fire the head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, chipping away at Humphrey's Executor. Now the precedent is gone entirely. While the Court separately preserved the Federal Reserve's independence in a 5-4 vote, the broader landscape of independent agencies has been fundamentally reshaped.
why_it_matters: The ruling eliminates a firewall that for nearly a century prevented presidents from punishing agency leaders who simply disagree with them. For a middle-school student who might one day work, vote, or start a business, this could mean consumer protections and competition rules become dramatically different depending on who wins the White House — creating an unpredictable economy where companies face whiplash regulation.

background_read: The Supreme Court follows a principle called 'stare decisis,' which means it tries to respect past decisions. Overturning a 91-year-old precedent like Humphrey's Executor is a rare and dramatic move — the 1935 case was decided during the Great Depression, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt wanted more control over agencies, but the Court blocked him.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) was created by Congress in 1914 to prevent monopolies and protect consumers from unfair business practices. Its five commissioners traditionally served staggered seven-year terms, with no more than three from the same party — a design meant to keep the agency above partisan fights.

During Trump's first term (2017-2021), the Supreme Court already chipped away at job protections for the head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in a 2020 case called Seila Law v. CFPB. The Humphrey's Executor ruling from this week finishes the job for most independent agencies.

Rebecca Kelly Slaughter (appointed by President Trump in 2018 and confirmed by the Senate) was known for focusing on children's privacy online and data security at the FTC. Her firing without a stated cause tested the limits of presidential power.

perspectives.description: Many argue that in a democracy, the president should be able to remove officials who carry out executive functions. If voters elect a president to change economic direction, appointed holdovers shouldn't be able to sabotage that mandate. This ruling ensures the chain of accountability leads back to a single elected leader rather than to a panel of unelected commissioners.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / Critical (Loss of institutional expertise and fairness)
perspectives.description: Opponents warn that firing commissioners for political reasons turns the FTC into a tool of whoever occupies the Oval Office. This could destroy the careful, long-term thinking needed to police complex markets and might even encourage corruption — companies could lobby to get a regulator fired simply for investigating them.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical (Legal evolution, not sudden revolution)
perspectives.description: The decision didn't come out of nowhere; the Court had been weakening agency independence for years. Seen through a legal lens, the majority's reasoning reflects a consistent originalist view that the Constitution gives the president all executive power, and that independent agencies are an awkward exception. Still, the speed of the reversal after 91 years shocks many legal scholars.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking (The next frontier — Congress and the courts)
perspectives.description: Now that the structural protection is gone, attention shifts to Congress. Legislators could try to pass new laws that tie presidential removal to specific reasons, but the Court's reasoning suggests those might also be struck down. On the other hand, states may increase their own antitrust enforcement, and future Supreme Court appointments could reconsider the ruling in a different political climate.
